title: Develop and manage a data collection plan to support an agricultural enterprise

lessons.title: Deciding what data the enterprise needs
lessons.html:
Data supports decisions

Farms generate huge amounts of information: rainfall, yields, weights, feed use, sprays, labour hours, costs and prices. Data is only useful if it answers management questions. A data collection plan sets out what to collect, why, how, when, by whom and how it will be used.

Start with the decisions

List the key decisions the enterprise makes and the questions behind them.

DecisionQuestionData needed
Culling cowsWhich cows wean light calves or calve late?Calving dates, weaning weights per cow
Fertiliser planWhat does each field need?Soil analysis, yields per field
Irrigation schedulingWhen and how much to irrigate?Soil moisture, rainfall, evapotranspiration
Enterprise choiceWhich enterprise is most profitable?Income and variable costs per enterprise
Labour planningHow many pickers are needed?Picking rate per person, yield estimates

Types of data

  • Physical: quantities, weights, yields, hectares, head counts.
  • Financial: costs, income, prices.
  • Environmental: rainfall, temperature, soil and water quality.
  • Compliance: spray records, animal treatment records, training and safety records required by law or by buyers.

Distinguish quantitative data (numbers) from qualitative data (descriptions, such as observations on veld condition or worker feedback). Both are useful.

Keep it lean

Collecting data costs time. Collect only what will be used, at the level of detail needed for the decision. A small, accurate, consistent data set beats a large, messy one.

lessons.title: Designing collection methods and ensuring quality
lessons.html:
How to collect good data

Collection methods

  • Manual forms and record books: simple, cheap, need discipline and later capture.
  • Mobile apps and farm management software: capture in the field with date, GPS and photos.
  • Sensors and automatic recorders: weather stations, soil moisture probes, flow meters, scales with electronic ID readers, milk meters.
  • Sampling: when you cannot measure everything, measure a representative sample, e.g. weigh 20 random lambs per group, or count fruit on marked trees.
  • External sources: laboratory reports, weather services, market price reports.

The plan document

For each data item specify:

  1. Name and definition (e.g. 'weaning weight = live weight at weaning, kg, unadjusted').
  2. Purpose and decision it supports.
  3. Method and equipment.
  4. Frequency and timing.
  5. Responsible person.
  6. Where it is recorded and stored.
  7. Who analyses it and when.

Data quality

  • Accuracy: calibrate scales, meters and sprayers; train staff.
  • Consistency: same method and units every time.
  • Completeness: no missing records; use checklists.
  • Timeliness: record on the day, not from memory at month-end.
  • Identification: link records to unique animal IDs, field names or block numbers.

Check data regularly for impossible values, such as a lamb weighing 300 kg or yields recorded for a field that was not planted.

Data protection

Personal information about workers and clients is protected under the Protection of Personal Information Act 4 of 2013 (POPIA). Collect only what is needed, keep it secure and use it only for its stated purpose.

lessons.title: Managing, analysing and using data
lessons.html:
From data to information

Storage and backup

Store data in a structured way: spreadsheets with one row per record and one column per variable, or a farm management system. Back up regularly to a second location such as cloud storage or an external drive, so that a stolen laptop or a burnt-out office does not destroy years of records. Control who can edit data.

Analysis

  • Summaries: totals, averages, ranges per field, group or month.
  • Comparisons: this year against last year, block against block, actual against budget or benchmark.
  • Trends: charts over time show improvement or decline.
  • Ratios and KPIs: yield per hectare, cost per kg, calving percentage, feed conversion, labour hours per hectare.

Example: a sheep farmer records lamb weaning weights and ewe IDs. Analysis shows that ewes in the bottom 20% wean lambs well below the flock average for two years running. Culling and replacing them raises the flock's total weaning weight.

Reporting

Present information clearly to the people who decide: a one-page monthly dashboard with key KPIs and short comments is often more useful than long tables. Report on time so decisions can still be influenced.

Reviewing the plan

Each year ask: did we use this data? Was it accurate? Is something missing? Drop items nobody uses and add ones needed for new decisions or buyer requirements.

Key points

  • Start a data plan from the decisions the enterprise must make.
  • Specify each data item's definition, method, frequency and responsible person.
  • Ensure accuracy, consistency, completeness and timeliness.
  • Back up data and protect personal information under POPIA.
  • Analyse with KPIs, comparisons and trends; review the plan annually.
